item.title: Musk's political baggage clouds prospects for SpaceX-Tesla deal
item.description: The possible merger may face bigger obstacles from politics than from regulation, drawing scrutiny in Beijing and potentially igniting a battle between President Donald Trump and the Democrats.
item.dc:creator: Cassell Bryan-Low, Hyunjoo Jin
item.content:encoded: A possible merger between Elon Musk's rocket company SpaceX (SPCX.O) and carmaker Tesla (TSLA.O) may face bigger obstacles from politics than from regulation, drawing scrutiny in Beijing and potentially igniting a battle between US President Donald Trump and the Democrats. Musk revived speculation about [USN:L4N4661IU TEXT:"a tie-up"] this week, calling a combination "a good idea" and confirming that committees at both companies were reviewing a potential deal, a step toward what could become the largest merger in history and create a company worth about $3.5 trillion. But a merger would also unite one of the US government's most important aerospace and defense contractors with one of the most China-exposed major American manufacturers — a combination likely to raise questions about national security risks both in Washington and in Beijing. Those concerns are unlikely to derail a deal, analysts said, but they would likely leave the combined company exposed to years of political wrangling and pressure from both sides of the Pacific. Tesla's China operations, they said, could become a source of leverage for Beijing in any future dispute with Washington, while a Democratic takeover of the US House of Representatives in next month's midterm elections could subject the deal to congressional investigations and political maneuvering. Democrats immediately raised concerns about the deal's implications, signaling their intent to turn the merger into a political flashpoint ahead of the November 3 midterms. “If Elon Musk moves forward with the merger of Tesla and SpaceX, the deal would carry real risks that antitrust enforcers across the world would scrutinize," said US Senator Cory Booker, a New Jersey Democrat who sits on both the Judiciary and Foreign Relations committees. He added that he was prepared to conduct oversight of any deal: "When one person controls the infrastructure that governments and militaries depend on, his business decisions become national security decisions, too." Musk could seek to address concerns by limiting how closely the two companies are integrated. The greater threat to the deal may come later, however, if a future administration takes a harder line on the relationship between Tesla and a company increasingly tied to US national security, analysts said. "A merger agreement would involve pledges of limits to the connections between SpaceX and Tesla," said Derek Scissors, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. "I don't think the Trump administration would enforce these limits. However, the next administration could certainly begin to scrutinize a merged entity. This may be the biggest risk to a deal - that it could get unwound in 2029." EXPOSURE TO CHINA For Beijing, a merger would effectively place Tesla's sprawling Shanghai manufacturing hub under the same corporate umbrella as SpaceX, a company that has become deeply embedded in US military and national security activities through its Pentagon work and through Starlink's role in conflicts, including Ukraine. "A formal merger would make it harder for Chinese authorities to treat Tesla as a purely commercial actor, raising risks for future factory expansions, data approvals, or market access," said Alicia Garcia-Herrero, a senior research fellow at the Brussels-based Bruegel think tank. Tesla's reliance on production from Shanghai already gives China considerable leverage over Musk's business empire. A merger could extend that control to a broader corporate group encompassing strategically important assets such as satellite communications, launch services and military-related technologies. GLOBAL REGULATORY HURDLES The deal would also have to navigate a maze of reviews around the world as competition authorities assess its impact on industries ranging from automobiles and satellite communications to artificial intelligence and semiconductors. Musk's close relationship with Trump would likely dispel concerns about potential US regulatory roadblocks to a transaction, analysts said, while antitrust experts see limited competition concerns because the companies operate largely in separate markets. Outside the United States, however, foreign regulators are likely to scrutinize whether a combined company would gain an unfair advantage by integrating technologies spanning automobiles, artificial intelligence and aerospace. Antitrust experts said authorities in markets with powerful domestic auto industries, such as China and South Korea, could examine whether Tesla's access to SpaceX technologies would give it an advantage that rivals cannot replicate, creating barriers for competitors and potentially undermining domestic manufacturers. Regulators could respond by requiring the company to license key technologies to competitors as part of any approval, said Ioannis Kokkoris, a law professor at Queen Mary University of London. A South Korean antitrust official told Reuters that the merger, if pursued, could require an in-depth review of its potential impact on that country's industries. "Korean antitrust officials will be wary of the merger. They will take the merger very seriously," said Lee Hwang, a law professor at Korea University and former Korea Fair Trade Commission official. "The stakes are very high in Korea because it regards both the automotive and aerospace sectors as strategically important industries."

item.title: S&P 500, Nasdaq end sharply lower as revived AI doubts ignite tech selloff
item.description: US stocks tumbled on Thursday and the Nasdaq posted its steepest daily drop since early June as a batch of high-profile earnings reports ignited fresh fears about the AI spending race.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Culp, Tharuniyaa Lakshmi
item.content:encoded: US stocks tumbled on Thursday and the Nasdaq posted its steepest daily drop since early June as a batch of high-profile earnings reports ignited fresh fears about the AI spending race. The S&P 500 ended deep in negative territory. But the tech-laden Nasdaq, dragged down by microchips, suffered a steeper loss, falling 2.6% in the wake of a spate of high-profile AI-related earnings results. The blue-chip Dow eked out a nominal gain minutes before the closing bell. [USN:L4N4671S3 TEXT:"Meta Platforms"]' (META.O) results beat analyst expectations, but its stock slid 7.0% as the Facebook parent posted its first cash outflow in more than a decade due to its AI-related expenditures and announced plans to issue non-voting shares in a two-for-one split to raise capital to spend on the nascent technology. [USN:L4N4671SD TEXT:"Tesla"] (TSLA.O) shares fell 3.1% even though the electric car maker unexpectedly posted positive free cash flow in the quarter and cut its 2026 capital spending plans. The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index (.SOX) , which has driven much of the current bull market's gains, plunged 6.7%, its biggest daily percentage drop since June 23. With Thursday's decline, the SOX is off more than 26% from its record closing high reached on June 22, yet it remains up 51.5% so far this year. The S&P 500 has risen 11.9% over the same period. "It's a wonderful day on Wall Street," said Paul Nolte, senior wealth adviser & market strategist at Murphy & Sylvest in Elmhurst, Illinois. "The only part of the market that is really suffering here is technology, which has been the golden child of the markets up until about June." "Investors are starting to realize that there are some holes in the AI story," Nolte added. "And that's having an impact on the indices because they're so heavily weighted toward technology." On the geopolitical stage, Iran-backed Houthis launched new strikes against Saudi targets, sending [USN:L1N46801N TEXT:"crude prices"] to a five-month high. Investors worried that ongoing Middle East strife could keep inflation hot and force the US Federal Reserve to keep raising interest rates. Data from the Labor Department showed [USN:L1N4680T1 TEXT:"initial claims for unemployment"] benefits kept drifting along near multi-decade lows. Signs of labor market stability will allow the Fed to focus on fighting inflation. Financial markets are currently pricing in the probability that the central bank will raise its policy rate by another 25 basis points before year-end. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) rose 11.89 points, or 0.02%, to 52,867.98, the S&P 500 (.SPX) lost 93.74 points, or 1.21%, to 7,663.43 and the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) lost 694.00 points, or 2.60%, to 26,008.86. Third-quarter earnings season is well underway, with 111 of the companies in the S&P 500 having reported. Of those, 83% have beaten analyst expectations, according to the most recent LSEG data. [USN:L4N46811U TEXT:"Procter & Gamble"] (PG.N) warned that rising cost pressures would take an increasing bite out of profit, but beat analyst estimates, sending the stock 5.6% higher and supporting consumer staples (.SPLRCS) . [USN:L4N4681XJ TEXT:"Blackstone"] (BX.N) advanced 8.4%, after the company said widening credit spreads on AI-related debt could present an opportunity to lock in higher returns. [USN:L4N4680XC TEXT:"Lockheed Martin"] (LMT.N) climbed 7.0% after the aerospace/defense firm raised its annual sales and profit forecast. [USN:L4N4680UE TEXT:"Spotify"] (SPOT.N) rose 11.1% after the Swedish music streaming firm forecast fourth-quarter profit above Wall Street estimates, betting on its AI-powered features to drive user growth. [USN:L4N46817V TEXT:"Union Pacific"] (UNP.N) gained 3.6% following the company's quarterly earnings beat, which was helped by core pricing gains, although the railroad flagged a hit from rising fuel prices. Chipmakers Intel (INTC.O) , AMD (AMD.O) , Sandisk (SNDK.O) and Marvell (MRVL.O) all tumbled more than 8% amid the broader semiconductor selloff. Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 1.01-to-1 ratio on the NYSE. There were 173 new highs and 366 new lows on the NYSE. On the Nasdaq, 2,022 stocks rose and 2,766 fell as declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.37-to-1 ratio. The S&P 500 posted 40 new 52-week highs and four new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 82 new highs and 342 new lows. Volume on US exchanges was 18.79 billion shares, compared with the 17.19 billion average for the full session over the last 20 trading days.

item.title: US banks are blocking third-party AI agents access to customer accounts, sources say
item.description: The industry has become increasingly concerned that sophisticated AI agents could harm the banking system and the institutions trusted to hold people's wealth.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Major US banks have been blocking third-party AI agents from operating inside customer accounts and making transactions, two people familiar with the situation said, following a report that AI agents were accessing bank accounts and taking actions independent of user instructions. The banking industry has become increasingly concerned that sophisticated AI agents could harm the banking system and the institutions trusted to hold people's wealth. An Axios report on Thursday said some AI agents attempted to take actions that appeared to be independent of user instructions, citing people familiar with the matter. In some cases, bank customers have shared their login ID and password with agents, with banks typically flagging and blocking those transactions, a person in the banking industry said. Still, such transactions cannot be deemed unauthorized if credentials were shared by the customer. Morgan Stanley (MS.N) has blocked third-party agents from accessing its platforms, but it had not seen any instances of unauthorized or rogue AI agents, according to a person familiar with the matter. Top banking executives earlier this month [USN:L4N45Z1M8 TEXT:"discussed the risks of AI agents"] acting on customers' behalf, with some warning the technology is adding significant risks for both customers and banks. JPMorgan Chase (JPM.N) CEO Jamie Dimon earlier this month said the largest US lender was developing tools to navigate the risk of AI agents carrying out tasks on their own. "We're not going to allow just any outside agent to come in inside the company because that's just too risky for clients and for JPMorgan," he said at the time. Charles Schwab (SCHW.N) CEO Richard Wurster earlier this month also said the brokerage was blocking unauthorized agents. "I get a report every day tracking how many times we've had to block one of the different agents, and it's not many because I think people aren't using it in that way in their financial life. We are blocking it because we want to have control over authentication and the experience," Wurster said.

item.title: Musk’s public endorsement of SpaceX-Tesla deal may throw a wrench in talks
item.description: Elon Musk's public endorsement of a potential $3.5 trillion merger has rattled some insiders involved in the discussions, who worry his comments could invite shareholder scrutiny and delay the process by several weeks.
item.dc:creator: Milana Vinn
item.content:encoded: Elon Musk's [USN:L4N4661IU TEXT:"public endorsement"] this week of a potential $3.5 trillion merger between SpaceX (SPCX.O) and Tesla (TSLA.O) has rattled some insiders involved in the discussions, who worry his comments could invite shareholder scrutiny and delay the process by several weeks, according to a person with direct knowledge of the talks. The disclosure created a "mess" for the process, as it could lead to questions about how well Tesla shareholders' interests would be represented, the person said. The concerns reflect similarities some participants see with Tesla's 2016 acquisition of SolarCity, which sparked years of litigation over Musk's role in the deal. Musk, who serves as CEO of both SpaceX and Tesla and owns significant stakes in each company, this week told investors that the two companies were examining what would be the largest corporate transaction in history and revealed that both had formed special committees to evaluate it. The backlash to those remarks is reported here for the first time. The parties have hired advisers, but discussions are at an early stage, three sources familiar with the matter said. SpaceX approached Tesla in recent weeks, and the companies have been discussing a range of transaction structures, including a SpaceX acquisition of Tesla or a merger under a newly formed holding company, the person familiar with the matter said. They are weighing different forms of merger consideration, including an all-stock deal, the person said. These details of the talks have not been previously reported. Tesla, SpaceX and Musk did not respond to requests for comment. SHAREHOLDER LITIGATION OVER TESLA'S SOLARCITY DEAL In related-party transactions such as a SpaceX-Tesla merger, independent board members typically oversee the process to safeguard public shareholders' interests. That issue loomed large in Tesla's 2016 acquisition of SolarCity, which triggered [USN:L1N36V3J9 TEXT:"years of litigation"] after shareholders alleged the world's richest man had influenced the process to bail out his investment in the struggling rooftop solar company. At the time, Musk owned roughly 22% of both Tesla and SolarCity, which was founded by his cousins. Shareholders argued that Musk's involvement and public support undermined the deal's fairness. Central to the case were [USN:L2N2OL1K9 TEXT:"claims that despite his minority stake"], Musk was a controlling shareholder of Tesla due to his ties to board members and domineering style. The Delaware Supreme Court later noted that plaintiffs' contention of the absence of an independent committee, together with "certain other facts concerning Musk's involvement in and public support for the transaction," warranted the finding of unfair dealing. The courts ultimately upheld the acquisition as fair, though it took several years for the case to be resolved and Tesla directors settled allegations for $60 million. MUSK CANNOT BE INVOLVED IN TALKS Musk owns nearly a fifth of Tesla and just under half of SpaceX, and analysts have said a merger would give him control of the combined entity. On Tuesday's call with investors, Musk acknowledged that as a conflicted party he cannot be part of the discussions of the special committees. Advisers are also in contact with his lawyers to ensure Musk is recused from the merger discussions, the source familiar with the talks said. Eric Talley, a law professor at Columbia University, said a merger could benefit shareholders by eliminating the need for Musk to divide his time between the two companies. He added that any legal challenge may be harder to predict than the SolarCity case because Tesla is now incorporated in Texas rather than Delaware. “The Texas thing is a wild card. No one knows how Texas deals with cases like this because Texas never dealt with cases like this,” Talley said, noting that Texas has sought to establish itself as a business-friendly alternative to Delaware, and Musk’s comments so far were not necessarily problematic. Ultimately, he said, litigation risk would hinge on the terms of any transaction. "Who's going to get the better side of this deal? And that's usually what gives rise to litigation," Talley said. MUSK'S COMMENTS COULD AFFECT DISCUSSIONS People involved in the process worry Musk's public endorsement of the merger and disclosure of talks could intensify investor scrutiny, as interested parties typically avoid expressing views publicly while independent directors evaluate a deal, the source said. The SolarCity case could become a reference point for investors and courts assessing any future SpaceX-Tesla transaction if advisers fail to fully insulate the special committees from Musk's influence, the source added. A tie-up between Tesla and SpaceX would be the biggest deal in history, creating one of the world's largest industrial and technology groups. It would surpass Musk's acquisition earlier this year of his artificial intelligence company xAI by SpaceX, which ranks among the largest corporate transactions ever announced. A deal of this size would also face scrutiny from global regulators, especially due to Tesla’s business in China and SpaceX’s work in US defense and AI.

item.title: Hacking attempts surge as companies, governments rush to patch PHP flaws
item.description: Global firms and governments rushed to patch critical flaws in the PHP programming language that underpins much of the internet, as a cloud firm reported millions of hacking attempts after vulnerabilities were disclosed.
item.dc:creator: Eduardo Baptista, Toby Sterling, Mariko Katsumura
item.content:encoded: Global firms and governments rushed on Thursday to patch critical flaws in the [USN:L6N467127 TEXT:"PHP"] programming language that underpins much of the internet, as cloud firms reported a surge of hacking attempts after the vulnerabilities were disclosed. The push came after governments in Europe and elsewhere took websites [USN:L6N4670DM TEXT:"offline"] as a precaution on Wednesday while website operators scrambled to secure systems running the software. The emergency shutdowns of banking, airline, rail, tax and government services from Tokyo to [USN:L6N467188 TEXT:"Helsinki"] mark one of the most dramatic tests of the decades-old programming tools that keep the web running, exposing how deeply governments and companies depend on code that few people understand. "I've not seen anything like this in a long, long time," Microsoft (MSFT.O) CEO Satya Nadella said at an event in Germany on Thursday, saying the incident showed the importance of building software that can be maintained securely as systems grow more complex. "It was a long day and a long night, I know, for all the IT and security folks." PHP KEY TO INTERNET'S FOUNDATIONS LIKE HTML, PYTHON The developers of PHP - a computing language like HTML and Python - released [USN:L6N4670ZW TEXT:"fixes"] on Wednesday for vulnerabilities that had lurked in the software for years until they were uncovered using AI. They urged users to "update immediately". Madeline Lawrence, co-founder of Belgian cybersecurity firm Aikido Security, said that details of the flaws had become public before fixes were ready, with attacks reported since. "Companies are racing to update against attackers who can use AI to exploit them. That's the whole race," she said. As companies and governments deployed patches and suspended websites as a precaution, hacking attempts surged into the millions, according to cloud services firm Cloudflare (NET.N) and Amazon (AMZN.O) . "In the 10 hours before it was publicly announced, across the network we saw thousands of attempts to exploit it," Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince said in a post on X late on Wednesday. "That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now." Amazon also said it saw widespread exploitation . IMPACT FROM JAPAN TO FINLAND Japanese companies including brokerage Nomura (8604.T) , lender Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group (8306.T) , airline ANA (9202.T) and East Japan Railway (9020.T) said on Thursday they were temporarily suspending some internet services as part of emergency measures. Brewer Asahi Group Holdings (2502.T) temporarily suspended certain websites and systems and was conducting a security impact assessment. Insurer Tokio Marine Holdings (8766.T) said it had suspended its group website. Japan's Ministry of Finance and Meteorological Agency partially suspended online services to implement safety measures, while Japan's National Tax Agency temporarily took down its service. The precautionary shutdowns show Japan's growing concerns over cybersecurity, as the country [USN:L1N45U0IU TEXT:"recorded"] more cyber incidents in the first nine months of the year than in all of last year, according to data from TrendAI. French telecoms group Orange (ORAN.PA) said it had temporarily suspended access to certain PHP-based websites and applications across several subsidiaries as a precaution. Tencent Cloud, one of China's largest cloud-computing providers, urged customers to install updated PHP versions but stopped short of calling for widespread website shutdowns. Finland's state IT services provider Valtori said it had continued installing PHP security patches overnight and was gradually lifting precautionary service blocks after [USN:S8N3WF054 TEXT:"shutting down"] government public web services a day earlier. "Restoring services can take days or even weeks, as in addition to updates, the systems need to be carefully tested," Valtori Director General Hannu Naumanen said in a statement. Valtori said the outages were not caused by exploitation of the vulnerabilities or by a cyber breach, and that it was not aware of any active exploitation of the flaws. SOME FIXES MAY TAKE WEEKS TO IMPLEMENT Several Asian governments ordered cybersecurity inspections related to the PHP vulnerabilities on Thursday. China's industry ministry urged organizations and users to inspect systems and upgrade to the latest secure version of PHP. It also recommended strengthening cybersecurity monitoring and changing accounts, passwords and keys where necessary. South Korea raised its private-sector cybersecurity alert level and activated emergency response measures, citing concerns over an increased risk of hacking attacks. Felix Kuhlenkamp, head of security at German digital industry association Bitkom, said that many larger operators had already carried out updates, but that for complex IT systems and smaller organizations it could take longer. "They may run a website using PHP but don't really keep a close eye on it," he said. "If a website is based on an old version of PHP for which there is no security update, the entire system must be updated."

item.title: Stocks drop as Meta fans AI worries, Treasuries gain
item.description: Stock indexes fell on Thursday, after Meta's earnings report reignited worries about the AI boom's heavy capital spending, sending investors to the safety of US Treasuries.
item.dc:creator: Caroline Valetkevitch, Amanda Cooper
item.content:encoded: Stock indexes fell on Thursday, after Meta's earnings report reignited worries about the AI boom's heavy capital spending, sending investors to the safety of US Treasuries. Brent crude hit a five-month high following Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia, which stoked concerns of further disruption to global energy supplies. The Nasdaq, weighed down by chip stocks, fell 2.6% in its biggest daily percentage drop since early June, while MSCI's All-World index (.MIWD00000PUS) was off 1.3%. Tech shares in Seoul, Tokyo, Amsterdam and Paris fell earlier. Shares of Meta Platforms (META.O) dropped 7% after reported quarterly results on Wednesday. Meta's third-quarter revenue beat expectations, but the company said it would [USN:L4N4671S3 TEXT:"issue"] non-voting stock, a plan that revived concern over its mounting capital commitments and the heavy spend of AI hyperscalers more generally. An index of semiconductors (.SOX) , among the biggest beneficiaries of AI spending, fell 6.7% in its biggest daily percentage decline since June 23. Shares of Tesla (TSLA.O) , which also reported earnings and cut its [USN:L4N4671SD TEXT:"spending forecast"], dropped 3.1%. Reuters reported that some Tesla insiders are concerned that CEO Elon Musk's public comments on a potential merger with SpaceX (SPCX.O) could invite shareholder scrutiny and complicate deal talks. Shares of SpaceX ended down 9%. Investors' shifting views over AI spending have added volatility to the market. The Nasdaq's Thursday selloff followed a 1% rally on Wednesday. "To the extent investors believe that those (AI) earnings are real... they are buyers of these stocks," said Rick Meckler, partner at Cherry Lane Investments, a family investment office in New Vernon, New Jersey. "But periodically, when they look at current earnings and the amount they're going to have to spend, they become concerned that these stocks are all overpriced." TREASURIES GAIN IN SAFETY PLAY US Treasuries rose, [USN:L6N4681A9 TEXT:"pushing yields lower"], as the stock market's fall boosted the safe-haven appeal of government debt. The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note was down 19.3 basis points at 4.953%, its biggest daily drop since March 10, 2023. It has dropped since rising to 5.3645% on October 7, highest since April 2002. Yields and prices move in opposite directions. "They are rotating out of techs, out of the AIs, and into the more safety trades, whether it's bonds or some of those big Dow Jones stocks," said Joe Saluzzi, partner and co-head of equity trading at Themis Trading. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) rose 11.89 points to 52,867.98, the S&P 500 (.SPX) fell 93.74 points, or 1.2%, to 7,663.43 and the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) fell 694 points, or 2.6%, to 26,008.86. MSCI's gauge of stocks across the globe (.MIWD00000PUS) fell 14.95 points to 1,122.93, its biggest one-day fall since June. The pan-European STOXX 600 (.STOXX) index fell 1.05%. BRENT JUMPS ON ATTACKS Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia raised concerns of further disruption to energy supplies from the Middle East, pushing Brent oil up about 4%. Brent futures rose $4.35, or 4%, to settle at $113.17 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate crude rose $2.32, or 2.4%, to settle at $99.47. Fragile equity markets also boosted the yen, while the dollar rose against the euro. The Japanese yen strengthened 0.75% to 156.96 per dollar. The euro was down 0.09% at $1.1222. CONCERNS CONTINUE FOR FRANCE French markets were again hit on concerns over the country's strained public finances and ongoing street protests. France's 10-year government bond yields surpassed equivalent US Treasuries for the first time since 2013, reflecting growing over France's deteriorating fiscal position and rising debt burden. The benchmark 10-year yield was last up 6.5 basis points at 5.06%. [USN:L6N46814J TEXT:"The premium"] investors demand to hold French government debt over safe-haven German Bunds widened to its highest in 15 years.

item.title: Russia bombs Kyiv and Ukraine fires drones towards Moscow, despite talk of renewing negotiations
item.description: Russia pounded Kyiv with ballistic missiles and Ukraine sent hundreds of drones towards Moscow on Thursday, as the warring sides kept up a barrage of attacks despite the latest US push to end the conflict.
item.dc:creator: Olena Harmash
item.content:encoded: Russia pounded Kyiv with ballistic missiles and Ukraine sent hundreds of drones towards Moscow on Thursday, as the warring sides kept up a barrage of attacks despite the latest US push to end the conflict. US President Donald Trump [USN:L6N4681B6 TEXT:"said"] SpaceX (SPCX.O) CEO Elon Musk had restored Ukraine's Starlink access, one of the issues linked to a rift between Washington and Kyiv that has cast doubt on US support for Ukraine. Ukraine said Russia fired at least 21 ballistic missiles in three waves. President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said three carried cluster munitions — "bomblets" that disperse over a wide area and are banned by many countries because of the danger to civilians. Russia's defence ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Russia said Ukraine launched 630 drones towards Moscow during the night. The two sides held an exchange of war dead, with Moscow handing over 252 bodies and Ukraine handing over 25, according to the Belta state news agency in neighbouring Belarus. Such exchanges have accompanied moves towards talks in the past. PUTIN: ENSURING SECURITY FOR RUSSIA, UKRAINE, EUROPE Russian President Vladimir Putin, interviewed on Russian television a day after meeting US presidential envoy Steve Witkoff, confirmed that [USN:L1N468183 TEXT:"Russia was ready"] to resume US-mediated talks with Ukraine next month. Putin said the aim of the talks was to ensure the security of Ukraine and Russia after the conflict was resolved. Witkoff, he said, had stressed that discussions had to extend to "the architecture of European security". "And I agree with that too. Well, let's see how things develop in the coming days." Zelenskiy [USN:L1N4670ZQ TEXT:"said he hoped"] negotiations, which would be the first since February, would take place early in November. Trump, in comments on Starlink, declined to say whether he had spoken to Musk about restoring the service for Ukraine. Earlier, the Wall Street Journal reported that Trump had called Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on Ukraine's use. "I don't want to comment on it, whether I called or whether somebody else called ... The bottom line - he put it back," Trump told reporters. Ukraine uses Starlink for battlefield communications and drone operations. Restricting the service hampered the country's attack and air defence drone missions against Russia. [USN:L8N4682IN TEXT:"Speaking"] earlier alongside Finland's prime minister, Zelenskiy said speed on Starlink systems had not been restored for Ukraine. "We are tackling that," Zelenskiy said, adding he hoped to discuss the issue with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. A person familiar with the Starlink issue said the problem was continuing, with the same curbs largely remaining in place. Some drone units report reaching speeds of 200 kph (125 mph) with drones but otherwise the picture was unchanged, he said. “The main problem is that we have no official explanation what's going on," he said. RIFT BETWEEN WASHINGTON AND KYIV In more than a week of differences between Washington and Kyiv, Trump has repeatedly rebuked Ukraine for attacking Russian oil refineries while saying little about far deadlier Russian attacks on Ukraine. He called for Zelenskiy to be replaced and said Russia's actions in Ukraine have been "fine". Zelenskiy, who long avoided any criticism of the Trump administration, has increasingly pushed back against what he describes as a shift towards sympathy with Moscow. On Thursday, Zelenskiy snapped back at Witkoff for saluting Putin as a "humanitarian" during his visit to Russia, when the US envoy thanked Putin for [USN:L8N4670PP TEXT:"releasing a 74-year-old American"] captured by Russian forces in Ukraine. "Three waves of ballistic missiles have been launched at Kyiv by Russian 'humanitarians' since yesterday evening," Zelenskiy posted on X. "They used 21 missiles. Unfortunately, numerous sites across the city have been hit and damaged." Zelenskiy's meeting with Witkoff was aimed in part at repairing frayed relations with Washington after Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel and lifted sanctions on Moscow. Kyiv says Washington failed to provide early-warning data on Russian missile launches, throttled the SpaceX satellite system used to guide Ukrainian drones, and withheld missile defence systems bought on Ukreaine's behalf by Europeans. Washington denies shifting policies to hamper Ukrainian forces. After meeting Zelenskiy and European and NATO officials in Oslo this week, Witkoff spoke of "some degree of momentum", but the Kremlin expressed doubts. "The Americans sensed some new nuances (in Oslo) and told us about this. But these nuances, so to speak, do not entirely satisfy us," Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said on Thursday. A senior Russian official, briefed on the Putin-Witkoff talks, said they were relatively short and not substantive. The American brought proposals drafted in Oslo and handed them to Putin for review, the person said. Another source close to the Kremlin said the US proposals included a scenario where Ukraine would cede its Donbas region to Russia in return for receiving a guarantee of its future security from NATO. Moscow has repeatedly said it would not end fighting unless Ukraine cedes more land, limits the size of its forces and is permanently barred from forming alliances. Ukraine dismisses Russia's conditions as a demand for capitulation that would leave it defenceless. ATTACKS IN MANY REGIONS Zelenskiy said two people were killed and 34 injured, including five children, in overnight attacks on a dozen Ukrainian regions. Regional officials said a Russian strike on a market in Lozova, near the northeastern city of Kharkiv, killed two people and injured 36. Three were killed in the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia and one more in nearby Dnipropetrovsk region. Russia said it carried out a "massive strike" overnight on port infrastructure in Ukraine's Odesa region, as well as on vessels used by the Ukrainian military. In Russia, two people were wounded near Moscow by drones launched overnight towards the capital, Mayor Sergei Sobyanin [USN:P8N44K018 TEXT:"said"]. Most of the drones were downed at long range, he added.

item.title: Trump backs Ramaswamy attack ad as Republican Ohio governor condemns it
item.description: US President Donald Trump extolled an attack ad by Republican Vivek Ramaswamy against his Democratic rival in the close Ohio governor's race on Thursday, even as the state's Republican governor advised Ramaswamy to take it down.
item.dc:creator: Helen Coster
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump extolled an attack ad by Republican Vivek Ramaswamy against his Democratic rival in the close Ohio governor's race on Thursday, even as the state's Republican governor advised Ramaswamy to take it down. In the ad, Democratic candidate Amy Acton’s estranged mother, Donna Arthur, disputes Acton's account of a childhood involving homelessness and sexual abuse and urges Ohioans not to vote for her. In a Truth Social post, Trump advised Ramaswamy to keep running the ad. While not referring directly to the abuse allegations, Trump said: “let everyone listen to the mother of a defective, dishonest, and incapable Candidate, explain how the daughter is a DISASTER who, uncontrollably, lies, cheats, and steals!" Acton says she has not seen her mother since 1978. Acton's brother has supported her account of being sexually abused by her stepfather when she was a child. The stepfather, who died in 2004, was charged with rape. Opinion polls show Acton narrowly leading Ramaswamy, and analysts say the controversy could backfire on Republicans ahead of the November 3 midterms. 'IT'S JUST WRONG,' REPUBLICAN GOVERNOR SAYS Commenting on the ad, Ohio Governor Mike DeWine, a Republican, told reporters on Thursday: "It’s just wrong,” adding he would urge the Ramaswamy campaign to take down the ad. As the backlash built on Tuesday, Ramaswamy's campaign spokesperson Connie Luck issued a statement saying: "We don't know what happened between Amy and her mother ... but we know that Amy Acton is a serial fabulist." Acton's brother, Philip Stearns, called the ad a “desperate, disgusting attack,” while Acton campaign spokesperson Addie Bullock called Ramaswamy's decision to promote it “both despicable and entirely predictable.” Vice President JD Vance, campaigning on Wednesday with Ramaswamy and US Senator Jon Husted, an Ohio Republican, had brushed aside the blowback. Ramaswamy’s campaign said it was spending $4 million to promote the ad. David Cohen, a political science professor at the University of Akron, characterized the ad as "campaign malpractice.” Cohen said it could also mean trouble for Husted, who said in a statement that he would "not have run that ad" and who polls show trailing Democrat Sherrod Brown in a race that will help determine control of the US Senate. Among Republicans, Cohen predicted, "I think this will either encourage some people to switch parties, or more likely, you're going to have a lot of people staying home" on Election Day.

item.title: UK consumer confidence tumbles ahead of Healey's budget, GfK reports
item.description: British consumer confidence has suffered its sharpest month-on-month fall since early in the COVID-19 pandemic as economic worries deepen, according to a survey that created an unwelcome backdrop for finance minister John Healey's budget next week.
item.dc:creator: Andy Bruce
item.content:encoded: British consumer confidence has suffered its sharpest month-on-month fall since early in the COVID-19 pandemic as economic worries deepen, according to a survey that created an unwelcome backdrop for finance minister John Healey's budget next week. GfK's consumer confidence index dropped 11 points to -24 in October, its lowest since April and below all the forecasts from economists a Reuters poll. September's reading of -13 was the highest since August 2024. The drop was biggest from one month to the next since April 2020, just after Britain entered its first coronavirus lockdown. Excluding the pandemic, the last drop on this scale followed the June 2016 Brexit vote. GfK said no single factor explained the slump and pointed instead to rising inflation, the conflict in the Middle East and the broader squeeze on household budgets. Healey has said he wants to give households and businesses "breathing space" in his budget. He has struck an upbeat tone on the economy, pointing to growth in the first half of the year that was jointly the fastest in the Group of Seven. But surveys this month from S&P Global and LSEG/Ipsos have also shown weaker consumer sentiment, undoing a recovery that took hold around the time Andy Burnham became prime minister. "The speed of this deterioration is alarming," said Neil Bellamy, consumer insights director at GfK. Households' views of the wider economy and their appetite for big-ticket purchases deteriorated sharply with the major purchase index falling to its lowest in more than two years. Consumers' inflation expectations rose to their highest since April when they reached an almost 3-1/2-year peak. That is likely to concern the Bank of England, which is expected to raise interest rates next month. GfK's survey of 2,003 adults was conducted October 1-14.
